sources.citation: Collins, James T. 1983. The historical relationships of the languages of Central Maluku, Indonesia. Pacific Linguistics D-47. Canberra: Research School of Pacific Studies, ANU. ix+168 pp.
sources.note: Comparative-historical. Contains Collins's own first-hand Seit and Kaitetu data (pp. 108-109: 'The first data ever published regarding Seit and its sister dialect Kaitetu appear here') and grammatical notes (Kaitetu genitives p. 28, Seit conjugations p. 25), but NO statement on Seit-Kaitetu stress. The only stress rules stated are for the West Piru Bay neighbours, p. 83: 'Stress in Hoamoal languages is always penultimate; if a suffix or particle is added to the word the stress shifts accordingly. In Asilulu this is not the case. The stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root word; a…

sources.harvard_location: Widener Library, call number Philol 14.7 vol.10
sources.note: Second-hand (van Hoevell 1877-based) stress statement for 'Hila'. On the identity of the variety: van Hoevell's/Stresemann's 'Hila' is the speech of Wakal, Hitulama, Hitumessing, Mamala and Morela (Collins 1983: 10-11) = Hitu (hitu1239); Hila village itself speaks Hitu, not Seit-Kaitetu (Taber 1996: 42; Travis 1989); van Hoevell published no Seit/Kaitetu data (Collins 1983: 108). Listed only so that this rule is NOT imputed to seit1239 via the Glottolog alias 'Hila-Kaitetu'.
